metrics.name: Time horizon of frontier AI agents on software tasks (METR, 50% success)

scenarios.name: METR long-run trend, doubling every 6 months
scenarios.note: The doubling time METR fits to its whole series since 2019, about 188 days, carried forward from Mythos Preview. It reaches a 40-hour week in late 2026, a 167-hour month at the end of 2027 and a 2,000-hour year in late 2029. METR's own projection (March 2025) was that if the trend held, AI agents would carry out month-long projects by the end of the decade. Above about 16 hours METR's current tasks cannot confirm any of this; every path here is a guess about what a longer task suite would measure.

scenarios.name: METR 2023-26 trend, doubling every 4 months
scenarios.note: METR's doubling time for models since 2023, about 129 days (95 percent interval 104 to 158 days, which gives the band); since 2024 it is faster still, about 89 days. On this path the horizon passed a 40-hour week in September 2026, reaches a month in mid-2027 and a year in late 2028. METR found GPT-5.6 Sol (June 2026) at about 11 hours if cheating counts as failure but 71 hours if cheating runs are dropped, and judged neither a robust measurement, and its May 2026 risk report said the best agents essentially saturated the task suite.

scenarios.note: The default run of the AI Futures Project's model on aifuturesmodel.com (read 28 October 2026), in which each doubling is 8 percent easier than the last (superexponential), starting from a 4-month doubling time. The model forecasts the 80 percent horizon; it is converted here to the 50 percent horizon at Mythos Preview's ratio of 5.6 (1,045 to 186 minutes), an assumption, since the ratio was 10 for Claude Opus 4.6. The run reaches an automated coder in late 2027 and superintelligence in late 2028. scenarios.name: Slowdown, each doubling 10 percent longer
scenarios.note: AI 2027's subexponential case, in which each doubling takes 10 percent longer than the one before, started from METR's 129-day doubling time. Growth slows to a doubling a year by about 2033; a month arrives in the second half of 2027 and a year in mid-2029. Whitfill, Snodin and Becker (2025) found that month-long horizons at 80 percent reliability come about 7 years later than a simple trend suggests once the shape of the success curve is modelled. Started from the slower 188-day trend, the same case would reach a year around 2031.

metrics.license: CC BY 4.0

metrics.license: Carlson's figures are CC BY-ND 4.0; the tabulated prices are reused as cited facts. 2026 point from Twist Bioscience's public price page.
metrics.note: Price to the customer of double-stranded synthetic genes, in nominal US dollars per base, as tabulated by Carlson (1999 to 2017). 2026 is Twist Bioscience's list price for gene fragments (https://www.twistbioscience.com/products/genes: "from $0.07/bp", rising to $0.09 for 3 to 5 kb and $0.09 to $0.23 for cloned genes); GenScript lists cloned genes from $0.15 a base. Short column-synthesized oligos fell much more slowly, from $1 a base (1992) to $0.05 (2017) in the same table; array-synthesized oligo pools are far cheaper, which Carlson (2025) puts at $0.00001 to $0.001 a base, but need assembly and error correction to make genes.

source.title: Epoch AI, Benchmarking Hub (frontiermath_tiers_1_3_v2.csv in benchmark_data.zip)

metrics.license: CC BY 4.0
metrics.note: FrontierMath is a set of unpublished, hard mathematics problems written by mathematicians, with answers a computer can check; tiers 1 to 3 run from advanced undergraduate to early research level. Values are the best score Epoch AI measured for any model released by each date, from Epoch's CSV (downloaded 2026-10-28). Epoch released version 2 on 12 June 2026 after fixing errors in 42 percent of problems and re-ran older models, so these values are higher than the version 1 scores reported at the time (on version 1 the best was 40.7 at the end of 2025, GPT-5.2, and 52.4 in April 2026). The AI Digest 2025 survey's median for the end of 2025 was 40 percent on version 1, almost exactly right (40.7); the Forecasting Research Institute's LEAP experts (mid-2025) expected 31 percent then, 55 by the end of 2027 and 75 by the end of 2030, all far too low. Epoch wrote in September 2025 that FrontierMath "could be solved as early as 2027 on current trends". OpenAI funded FrontierMath and has access to much of it. Scores saturate, so the straight-line trend is a poor guide near 100 percent.

metrics.name: Record fusion triple product in magnetic confinement

source.title: Wurzel and Hsu, Continuing progress toward fusion energy breakeven and gain as measured against the Lawson criterion, Physics of Plasmas 32, 112106 (2025), arXiv:2505.03834

metrics.license: Paper under the arXiv non-exclusive license; the underlying dataset (github.com/swurzel/lawson-criterion-paper) is MIT-licensed
metrics.note: The Lawson triple product n_i0 T_i0 tau_E* (peak ion density times peak ion temperature times energy confinement time, corrected for transient heating), the record for magnetic confinement devices (tokamaks, pinches, stellarators) by year, from Tables 1 to 3 of Wurzel and Hsu (2025) and their 2022 paper (arXiv:2105.10954). By their Table 3 (2022), D-T ignition needs at least 2.9e21 keV·s/m³ at 14 keV, and Q_fuel = 1 needs 4.6e20. The magnetic record has stood since TFTR in 1995: JT-60U reached 5.6e20 in 1998 and JET 2.2e20 in its 2021 D-T campaign, and the machines designed to pass ignition (SPARC, projected 6.2e21; ITER, projected 7.4e21) are still being built. The best stellarator is Wendelstein 7-X at 6.2e19 (2017); its 2025 long-pulse record had no published value at the time of checking. Inertial confinement uses a different triple product (n ⟨T⟩ tau_stag) and a different ignition condition, so it is not mixed in: NIF holds that record at 1.7e22 (shot N170827, 2017), and its shot N210808 (2021) reached hot-spot ignition at 1.6e22. After ignition the triple product stops being a useful measure for ICF; NIF's later shots are measured by gain (Q_sci 1.51 in December 2022, 4.13 in April 2025).

metrics.name: Remaining life expectancy at 65 by country income group

scenarios.name: UN WPP 2024
scenarios.note: The UN's medium variant. The UN publishes prediction intervals only for life expectancy at birth, so no band is shown. The world reaches 19.6 years at 65 in 2050 and 21.9 in 2100, about 0.6 years a decade.

sources.title: UN World Population Prospects 2024, demographic indicators, medium variant (CSV)

scenarios.name: Model: rejuvenation at the tree's date
scenarios.note: A simple model, not a forecast; every point is computed, none is data. Baseline (no new aging biology): the UN medium path for the world. On top of it, rejuvenation therapies (node aging-reversal) arrive in 2062, the tree's likely date; the band uses the tree's window, arrival in 2045 (high) or 2110 (low, which leaves the baseline unchanged to 2100). Effect: the aging-reversal criterion's 10-year reset, applied once to everyone 60 and over, so they die at the rates of people 10 years younger. On the UN's 2023 world life table that adds 7.3 years at 65 (my calculation). The added years are held fixed and scaled by the share of people over 60 who have had it. Uptake differs by income group, the point of the comparison. My logistic curves reach half of people over 60 8 years after arrival in high-income countries (scale 3 years, so 90 percent after about 15) and 25 years after in low-income countries (scale 6, 90 percent after about 38), with 15 and 20 years for upper-middle and lower-middle income (my interpolation). They are set from two past therapies. Combination antiretroviral therapy for HIV (1996): in the United States 53 percent of adults in HIV care were taking it by late 1997 to January 1998 (HCSUS), while in low-income countries coverage of all people with HIV was 19 percent in 2010 and first passed half in 2016, 20 years on, and only after generic drugs and donor programmes such as PEPFAR and the Global Fund (World Bank, from UNAIDS). Statins (first approved in 1987) had no such push: in 2003 to 2009, 66.5 percent of people with heart disease took one in high-income countries against 3.3 percent in low-income ones (PURE), and in national surveys from 2013 to 2019 still only 8.2 percent did in low-income countries (Marcus et al. 2022). The world line weights each group's uptake by its share of the world's people over 60 in the UN projection, so world uptake reaches half about 17 years after arrival.

In 2023: high-income (90 countries, 1.26 billion people, such as the United States, Japan and Germany) 81.4 years; upper-middle (54 countries, 2.81 billion, such as China, Indonesia and Brazil) 75.9; lower-middle (54 countries, 3.25 billion, such as India, Pakistan and Nigeria) 69.6; low-income (26 countries, 0.74 billion, such as Ethiopia, DR Congo and Sudan) 64.9; world 73.2. The gap between high- and low-income countries was 30.6 years in 1950, 26.5 in 1970, 24.5 in 2000 and 16.5 in 2023, closed mostly by fewer child and infectious deaths and, from the mid-2000s, HIV treatment in Africa. The dips are China's famine (upper-middle, 1959 to 1961), Rwanda's genocide (low-income, 1994) and COVID-19 (2020 to 2021). The UN and IHME both expect gains to slow; they disagree most about the poorest countries, where IHME expects much faster catch-up.

mechanisms.name: Automated coding
mechanisms.note: AI 2027's takeoff model put AI research progress at 5 times its human pace with a superhuman coder, and its authors' 2026 model puts coding uplift then at 20 to 32 times. Measured gains so far are far smaller: METR's 2025 trial found experienced developers 19 percent slower with AI, and its 2026 rerun about 18 percent faster, though it calls that unreliable. 10 times for software, once coders are fully automated, sits between.

mechanisms.name: Automated AI research
mechanisms.note: AI 2027's figure for a superhuman AI researcher: AI research 25 times its human pace. It speeds AI itself; its effect on other fields comes through the AI milestones it brings sooner.

sources.title: AI Futures Project, AI 2027 takeoff forecast

mechanisms.name: AI-led science
mechanisms.note: AI that makes discoveries on its own speeds the design and analysis side of research. Insilico reports 12 to 18 months from target to drug candidate against an industry 2.5 to 4 years, about 2 to 3 times, and beta users said one run of Edison's Kosmos did about six months of their work, though only 58 percent of its interpretations held up.

sources.title: Insilico Medicine, timelines to developmental candidate
Edison Scientific, Announcing Kosmos

mechanisms.name: Automated experiments
mechanisms.note: Robots that can run lab work and build things let experiments run day and night at scale. Across published self-driving lab studies, the median cut in experiments needed to reach a target was 6 times; each experiment still takes as long as its chemistry or biology does, so the calendar gain is smaller. Building gains more slowly, as robots have to be made and deployed first.

sources.title: Benchmarking self-driving labs (arXiv 2508.06642)
Szymanski et al., An autonomous laboratory for the accelerated synthesis of novel materials (A-Lab), Nature 2023

mechanisms.name: General AI
mechanisms.note: AI that can do any computer-based job speeds everything that happens on a computer and a little of what doesn't: better-designed experiments and trials fail less often (AI-discovered drugs have passed phase 1 at 75 to 90 percent against about 52 percent, but phase 2 at about the usual rate), and planning and paperwork speed up building and approvals. Economists who model this expect what can't be automated to set the pace (Aghion, Jones and Jones). The ramp is for it to be deployed and trusted.

sources.title: Jayatunga et al. 2024, How successful are AI-discovered drugs in clinical trials?
BIO, Clinical Development Success Rates 2011 to 2020
Aghion, Jones and Jones, Artificial Intelligence and Economic Growth (NBER w23928)

mechanisms.name: Superintelligence
mechanisms.note: Pure speculation beyond the AI 2027 figure of 250 times for AI research with a superintelligent AI researcher. Physical experiments still take as long as they take, trials need people to live through them, and building needs materials and energy, so these stay far slower than thought.

sources.title: AI Futures Project, AI 2027 takeoff forecast

mechanisms.name: Shorter aging trials
mechanisms.note: Once regulators accept a biomarker of aging as a trial endpoint, a trial can show benefit in a few years instead of waiting for disease or death, as surrogate endpoints have done for other conditions under the FDA's accelerated approval. Twice as fast is my judgment.

mechanisms.name: Cheap launch
mechanisms.note: When getting to orbit costs a few hundred dollars a kilogram rather than thousands, space hardware can be flown, tested and replaced more often, and built heavier and simpler. A half again as fast is my judgment.
